missions.title: Mars RAD learning cycles
missions.record_note: Sixteen cycles and one operator audit, each with a commit reference. The code of cycles one to nine is in the operator's working repository at the referenced commits; the code of cycles ten to sixteen is not, so their results stand as accepted and not certified until the cycles run again.

opening.spoken: The Mars RAD learning cycles, begun July eighteenth, twenty twenty-six.

short_version.spoken:
The system was asked to learn what drives the radiation dose measured by the Curiosity rover on the surface of Mars. It worked through sixteen cycles. Each cycle wrote down its question and its pass rule before touching the data. It assembled a full Mars year, about forty-three thousand real dose measurements across four seasons.

It learned four things worth knowing. First, dose at the surface falls during solar proton events, in every season. Second, solar activity pushes dose in opposite directions depending on the season. Third, in dust season the monthly average of solar activity matters where the daily value does not. Fourth, two bumps in the dose, in February and in May to June of 2024, line up with solar-wind disturbances arriving at Mars.

Two of those arrivals were flagged from the dose record first, and both were then found in independent spacecraft data on those dates. No catalog of observed arrivals covers Mars in 2024.

What it could not do is establish certainty. The fit improved season by season, but the system does not yet claim to trust any single relationship. And the size of the bumps at Mars is still unexplained.

What it needs from people is short and specific: dust data that has not been released, solar-wind measurements at Mars that will come from a future mission, a better filter on the existing spacecraft data, and a model that works hour by hour.

what_happened.spoken: The system was asked to learn what drives the radiation dose measured by the Curiosity rover. It worked through sixteen cycles, each writing down its question and pass rule before touching the data.

rely_on.spoken: the sign of the proton-event response at this site; the seasonal flip in the effect of solar activity.

do_not_rely_on.spoken: any dose prediction as certified. Fit improved by seventeen to forty-three percent depending on season, and that is all that is claimed.

stop.spoken: surface pressure as a stand-in for dust; daily-average solar-wind level as a driver; crude automatic arrival detectors.

new.spoken: two solar-wind arrivals at Mars in 2024, February 16 to 17 and June 13, each seen in two instruments on the date, and neither in any catalog of observed arrivals because no such catalog covers Mars in 2024.

certainty_statement.spoken: No relationship reached certainty. Two explanations are open: the model is linear and daily while the physics arrives in events; and the tolerance was set from the median error, which a review on October 5, 2026 found makes certainty fall even for a correct model.

preregistered.question: Do the seeded proton-event and shock edges hold? What is left over?

cycles.spoken: Cycle 1. The search space was committed before any data was fetched. About thirteen thousand eight hundred real dose measurements were loaded for the first window, May to November 2025. The seeded proton-event relationship came out with the opposite sign to what was expected: dose fell while proton flux was high. A growing over-prediction appeared in one season, from about one to about twelve and a half micrograys per day between July and November. Solar activity looked like the cause, but it fell just short of the admission rule, so it was not admitted. The gap was left open.

preregistered.question: Does solar activity explain the aphelion gap at daily grain? Does it hold near perihelion?

cycles.spoken: Cycle 2. A daily re-scan had been registered in advance. Solar activity passed the rule and was admitted. It lowered the bias by about thirty-nine percent in that season. A second window near perihelion, July to December 2024, added about fourteen thousand measurements. There the proton-event relationship was again negative, which contradicts an earlier benchmark from June that had it positive. Solar activity was admitted again, with the sign flipped: it raises dose near perihelion and lowers it near aphelion.

preregistered.question: Do event-conditioned forms carry what the daily index cannot?
preregistered.rule: five forms registered; top one admitted

cycles.spoken: Cycle 3. Five alternative forms were registered before being scored. Two were admitted with small weights and modest gains. The strongest signal, a recovery pattern after proton events, was runner-up and could not be admitted under the rule in force.

preregistered.question: Does the recovery pattern after proton events hold, with the predicted sign?
preregistered.rule: pcorr > 0 and learned weight < 0, both registered

cycles.spoken: Cycle 4. That recovery pattern was registered with a predicted direction, then scored. Both predictions were confirmed. Bias fell by about seventeen percent.

preregistered.question: Dust season: what do proton events do, and what is left?
preregistered.rule: no directional position on the sign; missing-sensor reading registered in advance

cycles.spoken: Cycle 5. A third window, January to July 2024, covered dust season and the big May 2024 solar storm. Proton events again lowered dose, the strongest of the three seasons. The remaining error here was not a steady ramp. It was two bumps: one in February, one in May and June. Every instantaneous candidate failed. The twenty-seven-day average of solar activity was admitted and gave the largest gain of the run, bias down about forty-three percent. The bumps survived. As registered in advance, this was read as a missing-sensor gap: the model has a dust mechanism but no dust measurement. The gap became a collection requirement.

preregistered.question: Does surface pressure, as a stand-in for dust shielding, explain the bumps?

cycles.spoken: Cycle 6. The one dust-related sensor that could be obtained, surface pressure from the rover's weather station, was acquired and tested. It showed no relationship, and the predicted sign was wrong. The proxy was refuted. This tells us the bumps are not shaped like column mass.

preregistered.question: Does true dust opacity explain the bumps?

cycles.spoken: Cycle 7. The real dust-opacity maps for that Mars year are not publicly released. The test could not be run.

preregistered.question: What should ESCAPADE show?
preregistered.rule: pcorr > 0 and weight < 0, registered about two years ahead

cycles.spoken: Cycle 8. A correction: cycle 7 had said nothing further could be tested. That was wrong. The MAVEN orbiter's archive covers the 2024 window. Also in this cycle, a prediction was registered for the ESCAPADE mission, about two years before its data will exist.

preregistered.question: Does solar wind at Mars, from the MAVEN archive, explain the bumps?

cycles.spoken: Cycle 9. MAVEN solar-wind data was acquired, one hundred and seventy-four usable days. Daily solar-wind speed had the predicted sign but was too weak to pass the rule. Not admitted. The filter used to pick out clean solar wind was crude, and the ledger says so.

preregistered.question: Are the stored certainty values corrupted?

cycles.spoken: Audit, July 19. The operator suspected the stored certainty values were corrupted. They were not. The stored history was a down-sampled display. One real finding came out of it: the internal certainty state can fall without limit, which is still an open design decision.

preregistered.question: Does an event-shaped solar-wind form do better than the level form?
preregistered.rule: top form admitted at pcorr >= 0.10; earlier results must reproduce first

cycles.spoken: Cycle 10. An event-shaped version of the solar-wind test was run with crude automatic detectors. It scored weaker than the level version. Not admitted.

preregistered.question: Does the rover's own optical-depth record cover the window?

cycles.spoken: Cycle 11. The rover's own optical-depth record was checked. Every public version ends about one hundred and ten sols before the window opens. Not testable yet.

preregistered.question: Do documented arrivals explain the bumps? Did something arrive around June 13 to 14?
preregistered.rule: two independent parts; circularity bar declared

cycles.spoken: Cycle 12. Using five arrivals documented in the literature, the event-burden form was admitted, the first admission on the solar-wind pathway. But its learned weight had the wrong sign, traced to a confound with a proton-spike in late May, so no relationship was kept. Separately, a prediction made from the dose record alone, that something arrived at Mars around June 13 to 14, was checked against MAVEN hourly data and confirmed: speed jumped at about ten hours universal time on June 13, 2024.

preregistered.question: Does masking proton days fix the sign? Did something arrive around February 17?

cycles.spoken: Cycle 13. A mask built from Earth-side proton data failed to remove the confound, because Earth-side instruments barely saw the far-side event. A second arrival, around February 16 to 17, 2024, was confirmed in MAVEN data on both the pressure and the speed criteria.

preregistered.question: With a Mars-side mask and the two confirmed arrivals, does the event-burden form hold?

cycles.spoken: Cycle 14. With a Mars-side mask from published records, the weight came out negative as predicted. Using the two confirmed arrivals as well, the form ranked highest of the whole campaign and was admitted. In the bump months bias fell by forty to sixty-five percent; the other months were untouched.

preregistered.question: What kind of arrivals were they?
preregistered.rule: criteria fixed before fetching magnetic-field data

cycles.spoken: Cycle 15. Magnetic-field data from MAVEN was added. Both classify as stream interfaces, not eruptions.
Cycle 16. A suspicion that the calibration period was contaminated was registered, measured at five thousandths of a microgray per day, and withdrawn.

findings.spoken: Dose falls during solar proton events at this site, in every season tested. The ledger's reading is that the dip in background cosmic rays outweighs the added solar particles here.

anomalies.spoken: An arrival at Mars around February 16 to 17, 2024, flagged by the system's own arrival register and confirmed in MAVEN data on both the pressure and the speed criteria.
An arrival at Mars on June 13, 2024, inferred from the dose record alone and then confirmed in MAVEN hourly data: speed jumped at about ten hours universal time.
Two bumps in dose in dust season that survived every public data source.

background.spoken: When a large disturbance from the Sun sweeps past, its tangled magnetic field acts like a snowplough and pushes aside some of the cosmic rays that normally arrive from the galaxy. For a few days the background radiation drops, then slowly recovers. Named after Scott Forbush, who noticed it in the 1930s.

mission_tie.spoken: it is the ledger's explanation for why dose fell during proton events.

background.spoken: Bursts of fast protons thrown out by solar flares and eruptions. They add radiation. At the Martian surface the atmosphere stops the lower-energy ones.
A steady drizzle of very energetic particles from outside the solar system. They are the main source of dose on the surface of Mars. When the Sun is more active, fewer get in.
The Sun's radio brightness at a wavelength of ten point seven centimetres, measured daily on Earth. It is a standard yardstick for how active the Sun is.

Where Mars is in its orbit, in degrees, which sets the season. The run divides the year into four quarters. Dust season is in the second half of the year. The ledger calls the third quarter the dust-season window and the last quarter the perihelion window.
The Radiation Assessment Detector on the rover. It is the dose measurement used here.
A NASA orbiter at Mars that measured the solar wind and magnetic field. The ledger says its public archive runs to December 2025.
A pair of small spacecraft to study the solar wind at Mars. The ledger gives the science phase as about 2028.

Where a fast stream of solar wind catches up with slower wind ahead of it. The gas piles up and the magnetic field is squeezed. Because the pattern rotates with the Sun it can come round again about every twenty-seven days.
How much sunlight the dust in the air blocks. It is not the same as how much air is overhead, which is what surface pressure tells you.
A way of asking whether two things move together after removing what is already explained by the drivers in the model. The run admitted a candidate only at zero point one or above.
Writing down the question and the pass rule, with a date, before looking at the data.
One Martian day, about twenty-four hours and forty minutes.
